15 Cyber Attacks Every Professional Should Recognize Before It's Too Late

Most cyberattacks don't begin with sophisticated hackers.

They begin with one click.
One weak password.
One unpatched system.

One employee who thought the email looked legitimate.

The biggest cybersecurity breaches often happen because of simple mistakes not advanced exploits.

Here are 15 of the most common cyber attacks every security professional should know:

1. Virus
→ Infects files and spreads to other systems

2. Worm
→ Self-replicates across networks without user interaction

3. Trojan Horse
→ Disguises itself as legitimate software

4. Ransomware
→ Encrypts data and demands payment

5. Spyware
→ Secretly collects user activity and keystrokes

6. DDoS
→ Overwhelms servers with massive traffic until they fail

7. Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)
→ Intercepts and manipulates communication between users

8. DNS Spoofing
→ Redirects users to malicious websites by altering DNS responses

9. SQL Injection
→ Inserts malicious database queries through vulnerable applications

10. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
→ Injects malicious scripts into trusted web pages

11. API Exploits
→ Targets insecure or exposed APIs to gain unauthorized access

12. Brute Force Attack
→ Tries thousands of password combinations until one works

13. Session Hijacking
→ Steals session tokens to impersonate authenticated users

14. Phishing
→ Tricks users into revealing passwords or sensitive information

15. Deepfakes
→ Uses AI-generated audio or video to impersonate trusted people


Attackers don't need 15 techniques to succeed.
They only need one vulnerability.

That's why cybersecurity isn't just about buying more security tools.
It's about building strong fundamentals:

✅ Keep systems updated
✅ Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
✅ Train employees to spot phishing
✅ Monitor networks continuously
✅ Secure APIs and web applications
✅ Prepare an incident response plan before you need one

The strongest security teams don't assume they'll never be attacked.
They assume they will and prepare accordingly.

Cybersecurity isn't about being impossible to breach.
It's about making every attack difficult, detectable, and recoverable.

How secure is the application before it goes live?

🔹 Broken Access Control
Users gaining access to resources or functionality they should never be able to access.
🔹 Weak Authentication
Weak passwords, missing Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), and insecure session management.
🔹 API Authorization Issues
Improper authorization checks leading to sensitive data exposure.
🔹 Sensitive Data Exposure
Credentials, API keys, tokens, and confidential information stored or transmitted insecurely.
🔹 Security Misconfiguration
Default configurations, exposed administrative interfaces, and unnecessary services that increase attack surfaces.
The majority of successful cyberattacks don't begin with sophisticated hacking techniques.
They begin with security gaps that could have been identified during a professional security assessment.

Given time, any and everything is likely to happen. Sometimes it just happens quicker than we thought.

The actions were identified by both companies and handled. But the matter of fact is that it happened, and it happened already now and not in two, five, or 15 years.
 
To me it almost sounds like OpenAI, and we as humanity, were surprised that this happened, at all. I think that, without too much stretch of the imagination, we should have seen this coming. 
 
Why didn’t we? What can we learn from it? What should we be doing next?
 
I don’t have the answers, I’m sure some of you will ha ideas and opinions about it (maybe we should ask an AI? 😊). But what I DO know is that RegTech have found a new “bad actor” to go after. 
 
That RegTech’s will be using AI to fight AI is no different from the past when people at RegTech’s were playing catch-up with people committing fraud, or money laundering, or any other crime. Most discussions around GHG accounting focus on classifying Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 emissions or applying the correct emission factors. Those are essential steps.

None of these replaces the others. Together, they help ensure that environmental information is reliable enough to support sound decisions.

As ESG reporting and climate disclosure requirements become more rigorous, organizations should invest not only in better carbon calculations but also in stronger systems for collecting, governing, and verifying environmental data.

Referrals Are Not a Pipeline
Revenue Architecture Series | $0–1M ARR | Stage 1: Legitimacy Architecture

Back after a week away, I got married. Back to work.

At the $0–1M ARR stage, most RegTech founders aren't worried about pipeline. 
When I speak to CEOs at this stage, I hear the same thing consistently. Referrals are coming in. The phone is ringing. Website leads are arriving. And when I ask about their go-to-market strategy, they point to all three as evidence it's working.

It isn't. Not yet.
What they have is inbound activity across multiple passive channels. What they don't have is a pipeline, because nothing is being systematically generated or converted through a repeatable process.
When I share this observation, the response is usually the same: why fix something that doesn't feel broken?

Here's what's actually happening.
The founder is reaching capacity. Every referral and inbound lead requires personal follow-up and deal navigation, all of which only the founder can do because the process lives entirely in their head. No outbound motion. No systematized referral process. No qualification framework. Just a founder running faster to keep up with inbound that feels like momentum but is actually dependency.
When capacity becomes the constraint, the natural next step seems obvious: hire a seller.
But when I speak to RegTech CEOs about that first hire, the profile they describe is almost impossible to find, especially in regulated financial services.
They don't just want a seller. They want someone who thinks like a consultant and speaks like a subject matter expert. The logic is understandable, but that profile is rare.
In this space you are not selling at a transactional level. You are selling a relationship first. That requires understanding the regulatory environment, how it applies across firms and how the solution alleviates compliance burden. Many sellers understand the transactional side. Far fewer understand the relationship side, and in regulated financial services, that is the only side that opens doors.
So the search goes in one of two directions: a subject matter expert who can sell, or a seller who also happens to be an SME. Both searches fail for the same reason. The role was defined around the founder's unique skill set rather than around what a structured sales process actually needs.
The hire fails. The founder concludes that nobody can sell the way they can.
And they're right, because they never built something that someone else could actually run.
Referrals are a signal. Website leads are a signal. They tell you the market wants what you're building.
They are not a pipeline, and not proof your process works.
When you made your first sales hire, were you looking for a seller or a version of yourself?

This is the project that came out of my 4-week journey into computer vision — and the real beginning of my dive into the machine learning world.

Meet TARIQ AI 🚧

It's an app that automates road hazard reporting. Here's how it works:
📸 Someone uploads a photo of a road surface 🧠 A YOLO-based detection model scans the image and identifies potholes 📊 A second classification model rates the severity of each one detected (low, medium, severe) and rolls it up into an overall severity score out of 10 🗺️ The report gets logged with its location and timestamp, and plotted on an interactive map so patterns and hotspots become visible at a glance

The idea behind it: pothole reporting today is manual, scattered, and easy to ignore. A system that can automatically detect and score road damage from a simple photo — and turn scattered reports into a geospatial picture — makes it a lot easier for the people responsible for road maintenance to actually prioritize and act.


Building this meant going from barely knowing what a neural network was to training and chaining together two separate models, wiring up a full backend to process and store the data, and building a dashboard to visualize it all end to end.

This is just the beginning of my journey with the ML world 🚀

🤔 If AI is so powerful, why isn't every Machine Learning model 100% accurate?

It's natural to assume that more data and more training should eventually produce a perfect model.

In practice, that's rarely the case.

Here's why 👇

🌍 1. The real world is noisy
Two identical-looking houses can sell for completely different prices.
Some things simply can't be measured or predicted.

🏷️ 2. Data isn't perfect
Wrong labels, missing values, and outliers confuse even the best models.

❓ 3. We never have all the information
Predicting exam results?
You may know:
✅ Study hours
✅ Attendance
But what about...
❌ Stress
❌ Sleep
❌ Motivation
A model can only learn from the data it's given.

🔄 4. The world changes
Customer behavior, markets, and trends evolve over time.
A model trained today may not perform equally well tomorrow.

The goal of Machine Learning isn't perfection.
It's generalization.

If you’ve ever wondered how AI learns from data, it usually comes down to three main approaches: Supervised, Unsupervised, and Semi-Supervised Learning.
Here is a simple breakdown to help you understand the core differences:

𝟭. 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮 𝗧𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿)
The Concept: You give the algorithm input data along with the correct answers (labels). The model studies the examples, learns the patterns, and uses that knowledge to predict answers for new, unseen data.
Analogy: Studying with a flashcard deck where the question is on the front and the answer is written on the back.

𝟮. 𝗨𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝘆 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆)
The Concept: You feed the algorithm raw, unlabeled data with no correct answers provided. Instead of making predictions, the model looks for hidden patterns, similarities, and structures on its own.
Analogy: Giving someone a mixed bucket of Lego bricks without instructions—they’ll naturally group them by color or shape.

𝟯. 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗶-𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲)
The Concept: You train the model on a small amount of labeled data combined with a huge amount of unlabeled data. It uses the small labeled set to learn the basics, then applies that knowledge across the massive unlabeled pool.
Why it matters: Labeling millions of data points manually is expensive and time-consuming.
Real-World Example (Medical Imaging): Labeling 1,000,000 CT scans for tumors would take doctors years. Instead, a radiologist manually labels 500 scans. The model learns from those 500 examples and automatically applies that knowledge to classify the remaining 999,500 scans to catch high-risk patients quickly.

Bottom Line:
Supervised: Data + Answers 
Unsupervised: Data only (Find hidden patterns) 
Semi-Supervised: Mostly Data + A few answers

Inside the Machine Learning Training Loop  
 في قلب حلقة تدريب نماذج التعلّم الآلي
Machine learning models learn through a guided trial-and-error process built on four key steps. They start by making a prediction from the data. Then they measure how wrong that prediction is. Next, they figure out how to adjust themselves to reduce the error. Finally, they make a small correction. This cycle repeats many times, so the model gradually gets better.
A simple way to understand this is to imagine someone learning to drive a car. In the beginning, they may oversteer or understeer, forget to use the indicators, or misuse the pedals. An instructor points out these mistakes, such as drifting out of the lane or stopping too abruptly. The learner then makes small adjustments the next time. With repeated practice and feedback, their driving gradually becomes smoother and more accurate.
However, unlike a human learner, the machine learning model does not truly grasp the meaning of what it learns. It processes information without understanding, following mathematical signals that guide it toward increasingly accurate predictions through a simple iterative process:
Error is high → adjust weights slightly → try again.
In technical terms, a machine learning model first maps input data to output predictions and computes a loss function to measure how far those predictions are from the true values. It then uses the chain rule during the backward pass to calculate the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight. This gradient tells the model the direction in which the loss increases. Using gradient descent, the model updates its weights in the opposite direction following the rule:
Weight at time (t) ← weight at time (t-1) – learning rate x gradient of the loss.
By repeatedly applying this gradient descent step over many iterations, the model gradually moves toward a set of weights that minimize the loss and improve prediction accuracy.

Started my AI/ML upskilling journey.
Until recently, I had heard the term Machine Learning countless times, but I never really understood what was happening behind the scenes.
This week, I started learning the fundamentals, and here's the simplest way I now understand it.

1) Traditional Programming (Data + Rules → Answer)
The programmer writes all the rules, and the computer simply follows them.

2) Machine Learning (Data + Expected Answers → Machine Learning Model)
Instead of us writing the rules, the computer learns the patterns from the data on its own.

The example that made it click: 
Imagine teaching a child to recognize a dog.
One approach is to give fixed rules:
• Four legs
• Fur
• Tail
• Barks
But these rules quickly break down.
• A cat also has four legs, fur, and a tail.
• Some dog breeds have very little or no fur.
• Puppies don't always look like adult dogs.
Instead, imagine showing the child thousands of pictures of dogs and thousands of pictures of other animals.
Over time, the child's brain naturally recognizes the patterns that make a dog a dog.

That's exactly how Machine Learning works. We don't hard-code every rule. We let the model learn the patterns from data.
How does the model actually learn?
The learning process reminded me of learning to ride a bicycle.
• Try
• Fall
• Learn what went wrong
• Adjust
• Try again
After enough practice, balancing becomes natural.
A Machine Learning model follows a similar process:
• Make a prediction.
• Measure the error.
• Adjust the model.
• Repeat.
This Predict → Evaluate → Improve → Repeat cycle happens thousands (or even millions) of times until the model becomes good at making predictions.
One simple lesson completely changed how I think about Machine Learning.
It's not magic. It's simply a different way of solving problems—learning from data instead of writing rules for every possible situation.

📚 Supervised vs. Unsupervised Machine Learning — What's the Difference?
Machine Learning is broadly divided into two types: Supervised Learning and Unsupervised Learning. Understanding the difference is fundamental for anyone starting in AI and ML.

🔹 Supervised Learning
The model learns from labeled data, where each input has a known correct output. Its goal is to make accurate predictions on new data.
Examples:
✅ Email Spam Detection
✅ House Price Prediction
✅ Disease Diagnosis
✅ Credit Risk Assessment
Common Tasks: Classification & Regression

🔹 Unsupervised Learning
The model learns from unlabeled data and discovers hidden patterns or relationships without being given the correct answers.
Examples:
✅ Customer Segmentation
✅ Product Recommendations
✅ Anomaly Detection
✅ Market Basket Analysis
Common Tasks: Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction

💡 Simple Analogy:
🎓 Supervised Learning: A teacher provides questions and answers. The student learns by comparing predictions with the correct answers.

🧩 Unsupervised Learning: The student receives only the questions and must identify patterns and group similar items without any answer key.
Both approaches are essential in modern AI—they simply solve different types of problems.

When you tap to pay, your phone communicates with the terminal using Near Field Communication (NFC)

But here's what's easy to breeze over: 

𝘠𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘱𝘩𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴𝘯'𝘵 𝘱𝘢𝘴𝘴 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘯𝘶𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘳

Instead:

• A unique payment token that's linked to your card is forwarded
• Alongside the token, a single use cryptogram helps authenticate

Together, the network token & cryptogram combo help make tap to pay both fast and secure

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗝𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆

Even though you paid with your phone, the payment still follows the same path as a physical card transaction

• The terminal (Adyen) captures the payment for the merchant 
• The merchant sends the payment request to their acquirer (Adyen)
• The acquirer routes the transaction to the network
• The card network (Visa, Mastercard) identifies your bank
• Your bank (Lloyds Banking Group) approves or declines the purchase

The approval is then passed back to the merchant, usually in a few hundred milliseconds

Today, UPI isn't just India's payment system — it's the world's largest real-time payments platform, recognized by the IMF, handling nearly 49% of global real-time transactions, and now live across 8 countries including UAE, Singapore, Nepal, and France.

From a roadside vendor to a multinational enterprise, UPI has quietly rewired how an entire nation transacts - one QR code at a time.

Most SaaS companies track churn obsessively.
But many overlook a hidden metric that's quietly costing them even more:
Soft declines.
Unlike hard declines, soft declines are temporary and often recoverable.
They can happen because of:
Temporary issuer restrictions
Network timeouts
Bank fraud checks
Spending limits
Authentication requirements
Processor availability issues
The customer hasn't decided to leave.
Their payment simply didn't go through.
Yet many businesses treat these transactions as lost revenue.
That's a costly mistake.
A failed renewal caused by a soft decline can trigger:
❌ Involuntary churn
❌ Lower Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR)
❌ Reduced Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
❌ Higher customer acquisition costs to replace subscribers
❌ Lost expansion opportunities from existing customers
The good news?
Most soft declines can be recovered with the right payment strategy.
Leading SaaS businesses improve recovery rates by implementing:
✅ Intelligent retry logic that schedules retries based on the decline reason instead of using fixed intervals.
✅ Account updater services to automatically refresh expired or replaced card details.
✅ Smart payment routing to send transactions through the acquirer with the highest likelihood of approval.
✅ Alternative payment methods when card payments continue to fail.
✅ Real-time payment analytics to identify patterns by issuer, geography, and payment provider.
The goal isn't just to process payments.
It's to maximize the number of successful renewals.
Every recovered payment protects recurring revenue without increasing marketing spend.
The most efficient growth strategy isn't always acquiring more customers.
Sometimes it's ensuring the customers you've already earned never leave because of a preventable payment failure.
Customer churn is a business challenge.
Soft declines are often a payment optimization challenge.

Every embedded payments relationship has two clients, not one.

There's the SaaS platform — the direct customer, the integration partner, the contractual relationship. And there's the merchant at the other end — the actual end user, the one swiping the card, the one whose business depends on the payment flow actually working.

When something goes wrong, the merchant calls the SaaS platform — not the processor. The platform absorbs the support load, the reputation hit, and the churn risk if the resolution is slow. The processor is invisible to the merchant, but the platform pays the price.

The payment partners that work best for SaaS understand this dynamic in their bones. They build for the platform's success and the merchant's success simultaneously — because they're structurally the same job.
